title: HCF & LCM
summary: Highest common factor and lowest common multiple — a small but near-guaranteed slot in CGL. Most questions are template word problems: greatest divisor with remainders (HCF of differences), least number with given remainders (LCM + r), bells, tiles and ratio pairs.

subtopics.title: HCF & LCM: definitions and core relations
subtopics.concept:
**HCF (GCD)** of some numbers is the largest number that divides all of them. **LCM** is the smallest number divisible by all of them.

- HCF ≤ every number ≤ LCM (for numbers ≥ 1).
- LCM is always a **multiple** of the HCF.
- For co-prime numbers: HCF = 1 and LCM = product.
- For two numbers: $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} =$ product of the numbers. (Does **not** hold for three numbers.)
- If one number and the HCF are given, the other number $= \frac{\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM}}{\text{given number}}$.

HCF of numbers close together is small (it must divide their difference); HCF of numbers in a fixed ratio is the scale factor.

tricks.title: Ratio split
tricks.body: Numbers in ratio $a : b$ (a, b co-prime) with HCF $h$ are $ha$ and $hb$; LCM $= hab$; sum $= h(a+b)$; difference $= h(b-a)$.

example.q: Two numbers are in ratio 5 : 6 and their HCF is 12. Find the LCM.

tricks.title: Product ÷ HCF = LCM in one step
tricks.body: Any question giving two of {product, HCF, LCM, one number} resolves by the product relation.

example.q: The product of two numbers is 1600 and their HCF is 5. Find the LCM.

tricks.title: Divisor pairs of (product ÷ HCF)
tricks.body: For 'how many pairs of numbers' questions, split product/HCF into co-prime factor pairs.

example.q: The product of two numbers is 2028 and HCF is 13. How many such pairs exist?

mistakes: Using $\text{HCF} \times \text{LCM} = abc$ for three numbers — false for three.
Forgetting that the co-prime pair (1, product) counts as a valid pair.
Confusing 'greatest number that divides' (HCF) with 'least number that is divisible by' (LCM).
Assuming the HCF of a ratio pair is the ratio itself.

subtopics.title: Finding HCF & LCM (incl. fractions and decimals)
subtopics.concept:
**Prime factorisation:** HCF = product of common primes with the **lowest** powers; LCM = product of all primes with the **highest** powers.

**Long division method** is faster for two numbers: divide, then divide the divisor by the remainder, repeat; the last non-zero remainder is the HCF. LCM $= \frac{ab}{\text{HCF}}$.

**Fractions:** $\text{HCF} = \frac{\text{HCF of numerators}}{\text{LCM of denominators}}$, $\quad\text{LCM} = \frac{\text{LCM of numerators}}{\text{HCF of denominators}}$.

**Decimals:** equalise decimal places first (write 0.5 as 0.500), find HCF/LCM of the integers, put the decimal point back with the same number of places.

tricks.title: LCM row of prime powers
tricks.body: Write each number as a row of prime powers; LCM = read column maxima, HCF = read common minima. Three numbers take under 30 seconds.

tricks.title: Fractions: numerators ↔ denominators cross rule
tricks.body: HCF of fractions = HCF of tops over LCM of bottoms; LCM is the mirror image.

tricks.title: Decimals: shift the point
tricks.body: Multiply everything by the power of 10 needed to clear decimals, solve as integers, shift the point back.

mistakes: Taking the HCF of fractions as $\frac{\text{HCF of tops}}{\text{HCF of bottoms}}$.
Forgetting to reduce to lowest terms before checking common primes.
Mixing up min/max powers: highest power goes with LCM.
Returning an integer answer for a decimals question (lost scale factor).

subtopics.title: Standard word problems (tiles, bells, groups, divisible numbers)
subtopics.concept:
Almost every CGL HCF/LCM question is a dressed-up version of one template:

- **Largest tile / rod / measure / greatest number that divides** → HCF.
- **Bells/traffic lights together, same starting time again** → LCM of intervals.
- **Least number divisible by each of a set** → LCM; greatest such N-digit number = largest multiple of the LCM within range.
- **Least number leaving the SAME remainder r** with each divisor → LCM + r.
- **Largest number leaving the SAME remainder r** → HCF of (number − r); if remainders are not given, HCF of pairwise differences.
- **Least number leaving DIFFERENT remainders**: try LCM − (divisor − remainder) when each remainder = divisor − constant.

Groups/military columns/planting trees in rows → HCF of the counts/dimensions.

formulas.name: Different remainders, N ≡ −c
formulas.tex: N = \text{LCM} \times k - c \text{ when } r_i = d_i - c

tricks.title: Subtract remainders, then HCF
tricks.body: 'Same remainder' questions: HCF of (each given number minus its remainder). Remainder unknown: HCF of the pairwise differences.

example.q: Find the greatest number which divides 85 and 72 leaving remainders 1 and 2 respectively.

tricks.title: LCM + r
tricks.body: 'Least number leaving remainder r with each divisor': add r to the LCM.

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 12, 15, 20 and 27 leaves remainder 5 in each case.

tricks.title: Bells: add the LCM to the start time
tricks.body: Convert all intervals to the same unit, take the LCM, add to the given time.

example.q: Three bells toll at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes. They toll together at 8 a.m. When do they next toll together?

mistakes: Adding the remainder when the question asks for the **greatest** divisor (that needs HCF of differences, not LCM + r).
Forgetting to convert metres to centimetres (or minutes to seconds) before taking HCF/LCM.
For 'leaves remainder 2, 3, 4 with 3, 4, 5' type questions, seeing $r_i = d_i - 1$ and answering LCM $-1$ only if asked for the least; other values are LCM·k − 1.
Using HCF where 'divisible by all' demands LCM.

subtopics.title: Two-step LCM/HCF cases (extra condition, N-digit bounds)
subtopics.concept:
The hardest CGL variants combine LCM/HCF with one extra condition:

- **LCM + remainder, further divisible by p:** write $N = \text{LCM}\cdot k + r$ and solve $N \equiv 0 \pmod p$ for the smallest k.
- **Greatest/least n-digit number with properties:** bound the LCM multiples inside the digit range first, then apply the extra condition.
- **Given HCF and LCM, reconstruct numbers:** numbers $= h\,a$ and $h\,b$ with $\gcd(a,b) = 1$ and $ab = \frac{\text{LCM}}{h}$; use the sum/difference to pick the pair.
- **Count of possible pairs:** count co-prime factor pairs of LCM/HCF.

formulas.name: Extra divisibility condition
formulas.tex: N = Lk + r,\ N \equiv 0 \pmod p \ \Rightarrow\ Lk \equiv -r \pmod p

tricks.title: Solve the little congruence for k
tricks.body: Once N = LCM·k + r, only k's remainder mod p matters — test k = 1, 2, 3, … until it clicks.

example.q: Find the least number which when divided by 6, 7, 8, 9 and 12 leaves remainder 1 in each case, and is also divisible by 13.

tricks.title: N-digit multiple scan
tricks.body: For least n-digit: divide the smallest n-digit number by the LCM, go to the next multiple. For greatest: reduce the largest n-digit number by its remainder.

example.q: Find the least five-digit number exactly divisible by 32, 36, 40, 45 and 48.

tricks.title: Sum or difference picks the pair
tricks.body: With LCM/HCF and a sum (or difference) given, list co-prime pairs of LCM/HCF and match the sum.

example.q: Two numbers have HCF 5, LCM 495 and sum 100. Find their difference.
example.solution: $a b = \frac{495}{5} = 99$, co-prime pairs (1, 99) and (9, 11). Sum $5(a+b) = 100$ ⇒ (9, 11) ⇒ numbers 45, 55 ⇒ difference **10**.

mistakes: Answering LCM $+ r$ when the extra condition demands a larger multiple of the LCM.
Listing factor pairs of LCM/HCF without checking co-primality.
Forgetting the (1, M) pair when counting possibilities, or counting (a, b) and (b, a) twice.
Missing that HCF must divide the sum/difference — a quick sanity filter for options.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Greatest number dividing with same/known remainders (HCF of differences)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the greatest number which divides x, y, z leaving remainders a, b, c' (remainders may be equal or different).
pyqPatterns.approach: Subtract each remainder from its number and take the HCF of the results. If remainders are unknown, take the HCF of pairwise differences of the numbers.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Least number leaving the same remainder (LCM + r)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the least number which when divided by a, b, c leaves remainder r in each case.'
pyqPatterns.approach: LCM of the divisors + r. If a further condition appears (divisible by p, or n-digit), write N = LCM·k + r and fit the condition.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Two numbers are in ratio m : n and their HCF (or LCM) is …'
pyqPatterns.approach: Numbers = h·m and h·n (m, n co-prime). From LCM = h·m·n work backwards. Then answer whatever is asked (sum, difference, LCM).

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Events repeating at different intervals, together at a start time, asked when next together or how many times in a window.
pyqPatterns.approach: LCM of intervals; add to start time; for 'how many times in t minutes' divide (t − first interval) by LCM and add 1 carefully.

pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Two of {product, HCF, LCM, one number} given; find a third, or 'how many pairs possible'.
pyqPatterns.approach: Use HCF × LCM = product. For pair counts, split product ÷ HCF into co-prime factor pairs (including 1 × M).

pyqPatterns.pattern: Largest tile / rod / measure / group size (HCF)
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Paving a floor with the largest square tiles, longest rod measuring all dimensions, biggest group of men/women.
pyqPatterns.approach: Convert all dimensions to the same unit and take the HCF; tiles needed = area ÷ tile area.

pyqPatterns.pattern: Greatest / least n-digit number divisible by a set
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: 'Find the greatest four-digit number divisible by 15, 20, 25' / 'least five-digit number divisible by …'.
pyqPatterns.approach: LCM first, then fit inside the digit range: subtract the remainder from the top bound, or step up from the bottom bound.

pyqPatterns.pattern: HCF / LCM of fractions or decimals
pyqPatterns.howToSpot: Bar of fractions like 2/3, 8/9, 10/27, or decimals like 0.54, 1.8.
pyqPatterns.approach: Cross rule for fractions; clear decimals and restore the scale for decimal values.

solvedExamples.q: The HCF of two numbers is 145 and their LCM is 2175. If one number is 725, find the other number.
solvedExamples.shortcut: 725 = 145 × 5, so the other must be 145 × 3 = 435 because LCM ÷ HCF = 2175/145 = 15 = 5 × 3 with (5, 3) co-prime.

solvedExamples.q: Find the greatest number which when dividing 85 and 72 leaves remainders 1 and 2 respectively.
solvedExamples.solution:
The required number divides 85 − 1 = 84 and 72 − 2 = 70 exactly.
$84 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7$, $70 = 2 \times 5 \times 7$ ⇒ HCF $= 14$.
Check: $85 = 6 \times 14 + 1$ ✓, $72 = 5 \times 14 + 2$ ✓.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Subtract the remainders, take the HCF: gcd(84, 70) = 14. (Option 83/17 ignore one condition; 8 divides both but is not the greatest.)

solvedExamples.solution:
HCF of numerators: $\gcd(2, 8, 10) = 2$.
LCM of denominators: $\text{LCM}(3, 9, 27) = 27$.
Answer: $\frac{2}{27}$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Cross rule: HCF of tops / LCM of bottoms = 2/27.

solvedExamples.q: Find the least number of square tiles required to pave a hall 15 m 17 cm long and 9 m 2 cm broad.
solvedExamples.solution:
Convert: 15 m 17 cm = 1517 cm, 9 m 2 cm = 902 cm.
$\gcd(1517, 902) = 41$ (since $1517 = 37 \times 41$ and $902 = 22 \times 41$).
Tile size 41 cm × 41 cm; number of tiles $= \frac{1517 \times 902}{41 \times 41} = 37 \times 22 = 814$.
solvedExamples.shortcut: Factor both: 1517 = 37 × 41, 902 = 22 × 41 ⇒ side 41, tiles = 37 × 22 = 814. (902 is the breadth — a trap.)

solvedExamples.q: The HCF and LCM of two numbers are 5 and 495 respectively. If their sum is 100, find their difference.
solvedExamples.solution:
Let the numbers be $5a$ and $5b$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$.
$5a \times 5b = 5 \times 495$ ⇒ $ab = 99$.
Co-prime pairs of 99 = 9 × 11: (1, 99) and (9, 11).
Sum: $5(a + b) = 100$ ⇒ $a + b = 20$ ⇒ $(a, b) = (9, 11)$.
Numbers: 45 and 55 ⇒ difference **10**.
solvedExamples.shortcut: LCM/HCF = 99 = 9 × 11 (the only co-prime pair with a workable sum). Numbers 45 & 55 → difference 10.
solvedExamples.pattern: reconstruct numbers from HCF and LCM

practice.q: What is the HCF of 96 and 404?
practice.shortcut: 404 = 4 × 101 and 101 is prime, so the HCF is gcd(96, 4) = 4.
60 is the only option divisible by all three (120 works but is not the least).

practice.q: The product of two numbers is 1600 and their HCF is 5. The LCM of the numbers is:
practice.shortcut: 1600 ÷ 5 = 320. Quick check: LCM must be a multiple of HCF 5 ✓.

practice.q: Two numbers are in the ratio 2 : 3 and their LCM is 48. The sum of the numbers is:
practice.solution:
Let the numbers be $2k$ and $3k$ (co-prime parts).
LCM $= 6k = 48$ ⇒ $k = 8$.
Numbers: 16 and 24 ⇒ sum $= 40$.
practice.shortcut: LCM of a 2:3 pair is 6k = 48 ⇒ k = 8 ⇒ 16 + 24 = 40.

practice.q: Find the greatest number which divides 70 and 125 leaving remainders 5 and 8 respectively.
practice.shortcut: gcd(65, 117) = 13. (Options 65 and 117 are the numbers themselves after subtraction — a classic trap.)

practice.q: Three bells toll at intervals of 9, 12 and 15 minutes respectively. If they toll together at 8 a.m., at what time will they toll together next?
practice.shortcut: LCM of 9, 12, 15 is 180 min = 3 h ⇒ 11 a.m.

practice.q: The HCF of two numbers is 29, and the other two factors of their LCM are 15 and 13. The larger of the two numbers is:
practice.solution:
The numbers are $29 \times 15 = 435$ and $29 \times 13 = 377$ (15 and 13 are co-prime).
Their LCM is $29 \times 15 \times 13 = 5655$ ✓.
The larger number is **435**.
practice.shortcut: Multiply the HCF by the bigger 'other factor': 29 × 15 = 435. (5655 is the LCM, not a number.)

practice.q: Three pieces of timber 825 cm, 675 cm and 450 cm long have to be cut into planks of equal length. What is the greatest length of a plank that can measure all three exactly, and how many planks result in total?
practice.solution:
Greatest length $= \gcd(825, 675, 450) = 75$ cm.
Number of planks $= \frac{825 + 675 + 450}{75} = \frac{1950}{75} = 26$.
practice.shortcut: HCF is 75 (both 675 and 450 end in 75-multiples). Planks = total length ÷ 75 = 26.

practice.q: Find the greatest number of four digits which is exactly divisible by 15, 20 and 25.
practice.solution:
LCM$(15, 20, 25) = 300$.
Greatest four-digit number = 9999; $9999 \div 300$ leaves remainder 99.
Answer $= 9999 - 99 = 9900$.

practice.q: The product of two numbers is 2028 and their HCF is 13. How many pairs of such numbers are possible?
practice.solution:
Let the numbers be $13a$ and $13b$ with $\gcd(a, b) = 1$.
$13a \times 13b = 2028$ ⇒ $169ab = 2028$ ⇒ $ab = 12$.
Co-prime factor pairs of 12: $(1, 12)$ and $(3, 4)$.
Pairs of numbers: (13, 156) and (39, 52) ⇒ **2 pairs**.
practice.shortcut: product ÷ HCF² = 12 = 1×12 = 3×4 (co-prime only) ⇒ 2 pairs. (Answer 3 forgets the co-prime check: 2×6 shares a factor.)
practice.pattern: count pairs from product and HCF

practice.q: Find the least number of five digits which is exactly divisible by 32, 36, 40, 45 and 48.
practice.solution:
LCM $= 2^5 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 1440$.
$10000 \div 1440$ gives remainder 1360, so $1440 - 1360 = 80$ more is needed.
Answer $= 10000 + 80 = 10080$.
practice.shortcut: LCM 1440; step 10000 up to the next multiple: 7 × 1440 = 10080.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 3, 4 and 5 leaves remainders 2, 3 and 4 respectively.
practice.solution:
In each case the remainder is 1 less than the divisor: N + 1 is divisible by 3, 4 and 5.
LCM$(3, 4, 5) = 60$ ⇒ N + 1 is a multiple of 60.
Least value: $N = 60 - 1 = 59$.

practice.q: Find the least number which when divided by 6, 7, 8, 9 and 12 leaves a remainder of 1 in each case, and is exactly divisible by 13.
practice.solution:
N = LCM$(6,7,8,9,12)k + 1 = 504k + 1$.
Need $504k + 1 \equiv 0 \pmod{13}$. Since $504 = 13 \times 38 + 10$, $10k \equiv -1 \equiv 12 \pmod{13}$.
$10k \equiv 12$ ⇒ multiply by 4: $40k \equiv 48$ ⇒ $k \equiv 9 \pmod{13}$ (since $40 \equiv 1$, $48 \equiv 9$).
Least $k = 9$: $N = 504 \times 9 + 1 = 4537$. Check: $4537 \div 13 = 349$ ✓.

practice.shortcut: HCF of tops = 2; LCM of bottoms = 27 ⇒ 2/27.

practice.solution:
Write all with two decimal places: 0.54, 1.80, 7.20.
$\gcd(54, 180, 720) = 18$ ⇒ HCF $= 0.18$.
practice.shortcut: Clear decimals (×100): gcd(54, 180, 720) = 18, shift the point back → 0.18.
